AMLC COMMENTARY - This week was one of the best for Australian livestock markets for some time. Rain fell across the southern part of Australia where it was desperately needed, numbers eased at saleyards, prices for imported product improved in both the U.S. and Japan and the South Korean government announced a tender, the composition of which should favour Australian exporters. These conditions enabled livestock prices to appreciate noticeably in both over the hooks markets and at the saleyards.

Falls of 25 mm to 50 mm were recorded in the southwest of Western Australia and through most of South Australia, Victoria and Tasmania. This is the second time in as many weeks that rain has fallen in these regions and, although it is a little early to have an immediate effect on pasture growth, it will form the basis for some growth as temperatures rise in spring.

Unlike last week, the rain did move into the southern and central parts of New South Wales (NSW). Districts in the southern and central slopes and tablelands and the Riverina all received falls of 25-50 mm.

As a consequence of the rain, cattle offerings eased in the southern states. Numbers were back by around 20 percent in Victoria, by around 10 percent in NSW, mainly in southern markets, and significantly lower in South Australia and Tasmania.

The news was also brighter in export markets and currently, compared to year ago levels, Australian export prices have improved across all markets by about 20 percent. Prices rose by 11 cents a kg to 367 cents for grassfed fullsets in Japan this week while in the U.S., although spot markets were weaker, forward offers for Australian product were slightly firmer.

The Korean tender announced on Tuesday was relatively large and weighted in favour of grassfed beef. The total requirement is for 11,046 tonnes, including 864 tonnes of grassfed fullsets and 6,420 tonnes of grassfed quarter beef. The 400 tonnes of grainfed quarters will also be of interest to Australian exporters.
Improved export demand and lower offerings at saleyards facilitated price rises of four cents to six cents a kg for bullocks and medium weight steers.
Cow prices also rose to two to three cents above last week's quotes. Feedlotter and restocker demand kept trade cattle prices relatively firm, despite lower demand at the retail counter.
These rises culminated in cattle prices reaching their highest levels in more than 18 months.
The Queensland cattle market index gained 2.3 points to reach 104.8 points, its highest since February 14, 1996.
In Japan, it appears that end users bought very carefully for the Obon holiday period currently underway.

Traders are anxiously awaiting sale results. If sales are favourable, there may be a scramble for stocks in the post-holiday period. This, coupled with an expected tightening of supplies out of Australia with the recent rain, could see prices continue to improve through September.

The U.S. market situation may be the trump card. Assisted by stronger end user demand and solid boxed beef prices, cash prices for fed cattle have remained at 65 US cents a lb despite continued large slaughter rates, heavier carcase weights and cattle on feed numbers.

Most analysts in the U.S. remain adamant that a price correction will eventuate if feedlotters persist in retaining cattle. Many cite the steep rise in carcase weights since May as evidence that this trend is strengthening. Some analysts say the bulk of cattle were marketed during July.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
